lessons.title: A next-token training target
explanation: A language model learns the next token at every position, using the preceding tokens as context.
`tokens[:-1]` excludes the last token; `tokens[1:]` excludes the first. Both lists have equal length.

learn.misconception: The target is shifted by one token, not a copy of the input.
learn.overview: A language model learns the next token at every position, using the preceding tokens as context.
goals: Construct equally long input and target lists, with each target one position ahead of its input.
Write the input/target pairs for five token IDs. Explain why both lists have four entries.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: Training text already contains its own answers: after each prefix, the next token in the text is the target. A token is a text unit represented here by an integer ID.
Later, causal attention lets each position use its available prefix, and the loss compares that position’s vocabulary scores with its shifted target.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Construct equally long input and target lists, with each target one position ahead of its input.
Copying the inputs would teach copying the current token. Shifting by one teaches continuation. The final token has no following answer, so it is excluded from the inputs.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: For [3,8,2,9], use inputs [3,8,2] and targets [8,2,9]. Position 1 predicts 2 from the prefix [3,8]; it does not predict from 8 alone. The result is one pair containing two lists.
`tokens[:-1]` excludes the last token; `tokens[1:]` excludes the first. Both lists have equal length.
sections.code:
def solve(tokens):
    return tokens[:-1], tokens[1:]

learn.takeaway: Construct equally long input and target lists, with each target one position ahead of its input.
learn.tryIt: Write the input/target pairs for five token IDs. Explain why both lists have four entries.

lessons.title: Only the available context
explanation: Autoregressive generation can use only tokens that already exist.
`tokens[-limit:]` takes the final limit items. A positive limit bounds the context.

learn.misconception: A context window does not include a future target token.
learn.overview: Autoregressive generation can use only tokens that already exist.
goals: Select the most recent tokens that fit within a positive context limit.
Compare a context limit of 1 with a limit larger than the sequence. What information survives each?

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: A generator repeatedly extends a sequence. Its stored history can grow longer than the number of positions the model supports in one forward pass.
During generation, keep the complete history for the returned text and pass only its cropped suffix into the model.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Select the most recent tokens that fit within a positive context limit.
The latest tokens are nearest to the continuation being predicted. Cropping limits computation and respects the model’s position capacity, although older information is lost.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: With [1,2,3,4] and limit 2, the model sees [3,4]. With a limit larger than the list, slicing returns the entire list. Cropping does not create new tokens.
`tokens[-limit:]` takes the final limit items. A positive limit bounds the context.
sections.code:
def solve(tokens, limit):
    return tokens[-limit:]

learn.takeaway: Select the most recent tokens that fit within a positive context limit.
learn.tryIt: Compare a context limit of 1 with a limit larger than the sequence. What information survives each?

lessons.title: From counts to probabilities
explanation: A next-token distribution assigns nonnegative probabilities that sum to one.
`sum(counts)` is the total number of observations. Divide each count by that total.

learn.misconception: The largest count is not itself a probability.
learn.overview: A next-token distribution assigns nonnegative probabilities that sum to one.
goals: Turn nonnegative counts with a positive total into a probability distribution.
Double every count and predict the probabilities. Then add one observation to just one candidate.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: Before learning neural scores, consider a model that counts observed continuations. Counts express frequency, but their total depends on how many observations you collected.
A neural model later produces logits rather than counts. Softmax is the different normalization we will use for those unrestricted scores.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Turn nonnegative counts with a positive total into a probability distribution.
Dividing by the total preserves relative frequency while making all entries sum to one. Dividing by the largest count would not produce a normalized distribution.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: Counts [1,3] mean four observations: one for the first candidate and three for the second. Their probabilities are 1/4 and 3/4; multiplying both counts by ten changes neither probability.
`sum(counts)` is the total number of observations. Divide each count by that total.

learn.takeaway: Turn nonnegative counts with a positive total into a probability distribution.
learn.tryIt: Double every count and predict the probabilities. Then add one observation to just one candidate.

steps.label: From counts to probabilities
steps.detail: Turn nonnegative counts with a positive total into a probability distribution.

example.code:
def solve(counts):
    total = sum(counts)
    return [count / total for count in counts]

print(solve([1,3]))

prediction.code:
def solve(counts):
    total = sum(counts)

lessons.title: Build a deterministic vocabulary
explanation: A vocabulary gives each distinct token a stable integer ID.

explanation: A training sample needs context_length input tokens and the following targets. Stride controls the start positions.

learn.misconception: The final input window is invalid if it has no next-token target.

goals: Build input/target windows at starts determined by a positive stride.
Change only the stride from two to one. List the new starts and identify overlapping tokens.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: A long token stream cannot be fed as one unlimited training example. We cut it into bounded contexts, each with a corresponding one-position-shifted target sequence.
This is the shifted-target contract applied repeatedly to a corpus. The Dataset will expose these pairs and the DataLoader will batch them.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Build input/target windows at starts determined by a positive stride.
A context of length L needs L+1 stream tokens to supply its final target. Stride controls the gap between starts; smaller strides create more overlapping examples.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: For [0,1,2,3,4], length 2 and stride 2, starts 0 and 2 give ([0,1],[1,2]) and ([2,3],[3,4]). A start at 4 lacks enough following tokens.
`range(0,len(ids)-length,stride)` leaves enough space for the shifted target.
sections.code:
def solve(ids, length, stride):
    return [(ids[i:i+length], ids[i+1:i+length+1]) for i in range(0,len(ids)-length,stride)]

lessons.title: A module owns a forward operation
explanation: An nn.Module groups parameters and defines computation in forward. Calling the instance runs forward.
`super().__init__()` initializes registration. `self.bias` is a Parameter; `layer(x)` calls forward rather than reading a field.

learn.misconception: Define forward; do not override __call__ to bypass module hooks.
learn.overview: An nn.Module groups parameters and defines computation in forward. Calling the instance runs forward.
goals: Call a small module whose forward computation adds a registered learned bias.
Point to the line that creates stored state and the line that computes a result for a particular input.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: An LLM contains many layers, each with state and a computation. nn.Module provides a common Python object structure for nesting and discovering those layers.
Attention layers, transformer blocks, and the complete GPT will all use this state-plus-forward pattern.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Call a small module whose forward computation adds a registered learned bias.
super().__init__ prepares Module’s registration machinery. Assigning a Parameter to self.bias registers the weight; defining forward specifies how inputs use it.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: Bias(3.) owns a scalar parameter. Calling that object on [1.,2.] executes forward and returns [4.,5.]. The module is the reusable object; the output is a tensor from one call.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits

def solve(q, k, v):
    scores = (q @ k.transpose(-2,-1)) / (q.shape[-1] ** 0.5)
    mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(scores.shape[-2:],dtype=torch.bool),diagonal=1)
    weights = torch.softmax(scores.masked_fill(mask,float("-inf")),dim=-1)
    return weights @ v

explanation: Autograd records operations on tensors that require gradients so derivatives can be computed later.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: Training needs to know how a small change to a weight would affect the loss. Autograd records a computation graph so PyTorch can calculate those derivatives automatically.
Model parameters use the same tracking mechanism. An optimizer later consumes their gradients to change their values.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Create a fresh gradient-tracked leaf tensor and differentiate a scalar computation.
clone copies values, detach disconnects earlier history, and requires_grad_(True) starts tracking from that fresh leaf. backward follows recorded operations and stores leaf derivatives in .grad.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: If a tracked scalar x=3 is squared, the output is 9 and its derivative with respect to x is 6. The derivative describes local sensitivity; it is not the output or a weight update.
`clone().detach().requires_grad_(True)` makes a fresh tracked leaf; `.backward()` differentiates a scalar result.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: A leaf tensor’s .grad is a storage buffer. PyTorch adds each backward contribution into that buffer rather than assuming the previous value should be discarded.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why

explanation: Evaluation can skip graph recording to reduce memory when derivatives are not needed. This is separate from dropout mode.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: Inference and validation usually need predictions without derivatives. Recording every operation for a backward pass then consumes memory without serving the task.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: Manually applying softmax, selecting targets, and taking logs can be awkward and numerically fragile. PyTorch provides their stable classification-loss combination.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea

`F.cross_entropy(logits,targets)` accepts unnormalized [items,classes] logits and integer [items] labels.

lessons.title: Flatten batch and time for loss
explanation: Every batch/time position contributes one vocabulary classification target. Flattening preserves their matching order.
`logits.reshape(-1,logits.shape[-1])` keeps vocabulary intact; `targets.reshape(-1)` flattens corresponding labels.

learn.misconception: Flattening the vocabulary into the example dimension destroys the class axis.
learn.overview: Every batch/time position contributes one vocabulary classification target. Flattening preserves their matching order.
goals: Combine batch and time into one item axis without disturbing vocabulary entries or target alignment.
Number the batch/time positions by hand and check that flattened logits and labels use the same order.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: A language model returns predictions for every example and time position, while the simple cross-entropy interface expects a table of prediction items and classes.
This allows one loss call to train all causally masked positions in parallel, rather than running a separate training update for each token.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Combine batch and time into one item axis without disturbing vocabulary entries or target alignment.
Flatten logits to [batch*time,vocabulary] and targets to [batch*time] in the same order. Flattening vocabulary too would destroy which scores belong to one prediction.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: For two sequences of length three, there are six supervised positions. A [2,3,5] logit tensor becomes [6,5], and its [2,3] targets become six matching indices.
`logits.reshape(-1,logits.shape[-1])` keeps vocabulary intact; `targets.reshape(-1)` flattens corresponding labels.

lessons.title: Convert loss into perplexity
explanation: Perplexity is the exponential of average natural-log token loss; lower values indicate less surprise on that dataset.
`math.exp(loss)` maps average cross-entropy to perplexity. It is meaningful only for comparable tokenizations and evaluation data.

learn.misconception: A lower training perplexity alone does not prove generalization.
learn.overview: Perplexity is the exponential of average natural-log token loss; lower values indicate less surprise on that dataset.
goals: Exponentiate average natural-log loss to obtain perplexity.
Compute perplexity for two losses and explain why changing tokenization complicates their comparison.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: Average log loss is useful for optimization but can be hard to interpret. Perplexity expresses the same token-prediction uncertainty on an exponential scale.
Perplexity measures token prediction on a particular dataset; it does not directly establish instruction-following quality or correctness of generated claims.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Exponentiate average natural-log loss to obtain perplexity.
Because loss is the average negative log probability, exp(loss) is the inverse geometric mean of correct-token probabilities. Comparisons need matching tokenization and evaluation data.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: A loss of zero gives perplexity 1. A loss of log(2) gives perplexity 2, matching the uncertainty of a uniform two-choice prediction in that simple setting.
`math.exp(loss)` maps average cross-entropy to perplexity. It is meaningful only for comparable tokenizations and evaluation data.

def solve(loss):

lessons.title: Keep validation out of training
explanation: A held-out split measures behavior on text not used for parameter updates. Split before sampling overlapping windows.
For a contiguous text stream, slice at one boundary first; only then build windows within each side.

learn.misconception: Randomly splitting heavily overlapping windows can leak almost identical text into validation.
learn.overview: A held-out split measures behavior on text not used for parameter updates. Split before sampling overlapping windows.
goals: Split a token stream into disjoint training and validation portions before constructing windows.
Draw two overlapping windows and show how a random split between them could leak shared content.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: Training loss measures fit to examples used for updates. To learn whether behavior extends beyond those examples, validation text must remain outside training.
This boundary is a first protection against leakage. Dataset design also needs to consider repeated documents and near-duplicates.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why

lessons.title: AdamW owns parameter updates
explanation: AdamW combines adaptive gradient estimates with decoupled weight decay. Its state must be saved to resume the same training process.
`torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(),lr=rate)` discovers registered parameters. zero_grad, backward, step keep the same ordering.

learn.misconception: AdamW needs gradient history as well as current weights for exact resumption.
learn.overview: AdamW combines adaptive gradient estimates with decoupled weight decay. Its state must be saved to resume the same training process.
goals: Create AdamW over registered model parameters with a specified learning rate.
Separate the information needed for inference from the additional state needed to resume an AdamW run.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: Plain SGD applies the same learning-rate rule to every parameter. LLM training commonly uses an optimizer that adapts update scales using running gradient statistics.
Resuming the same training process requires optimizer state and schedule position as well as model weights.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Create AdamW over registered model parameters with a specified learning rate.
AdamW tracks first- and second-moment estimates and applies decoupled weight decay. The optimizer therefore owns persistent state beyond the model’s weights.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: model.parameters() supplies the registered tensors. The training sequence still clears gradients, computes loss, calls backward, and calls step; constructing AdamW alone changes no weights.
`torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(),lr=rate)` discovers registered parameters. zero_grad, backward, step keep the same ordering.
sections.code:
def solve(initial, rate):
    weight = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(float(initial)))
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW([weight],lr=rate,weight_decay=0.)
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    (weight**2).backward()
    optimizer.step()
    return weight.item()

learn.takeaway: Create AdamW over registered model parameters with a specified learning rate.
learn.tryIt: Separate the information needed for inference from the additional state needed to resume an AdamW run.

lessons.title: Model state is named tensors
explanation: A state_dict contains named parameter and persistent-buffer values. A snapshot needs cloned tensors if the model will keep changing.
`{name:value.clone() for name,value in model.state_dict().items()}` copies tensor values for a stable in-memory snapshot.

learn.misconception: A state dictionary is not the model architecture; reconstruct compatible layers before loading.
learn.overview: A state_dict contains named parameter and persistent-buffer values. A snapshot needs cloned tensors if the model will keep changing.
goals: Take a stable in-memory snapshot of model state values.
Explain the difference between copying a dictionary and cloning every tensor value inside it.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: A model object includes Python behavior and numerical state. A state dictionary gives named access to registered parameters and persistent buffers for saving or comparison.
Snapshots support best-validation checkpoints and exact before/after comparisons without storing an entire executable model object.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Take a stable in-memory snapshot of model state values.
The dictionary returned by state_dict is shallow and its tensor values can share storage with the model. Clone each value if later training must not change the snapshot.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: If a weight is initially 2 and training later changes it to 3, a cloned snapshot must still contain 2. Merely assigning another dictionary variable does not copy the tensor’s storage.
`{name:value.clone() for name,value in model.state_dict().items()}` copies tensor values for a stable in-memory snapshot.
sections.code:
def solve(model):
    return {name:value.clone() for name,value in model.state_dict().items()}

learn.takeaway: Take a stable in-memory snapshot of model state values.
learn.tryIt: Explain the difference between copying a dictionary and cloning every tensor value inside it.

steps.label: Model state is named tensors
steps.detail: Take a stable in-memory snapshot of model state values.

example.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
def fixed_linear(value):
    layer = nn.Linear(1,1)
    with torch.no_grad():
        layer.weight.fill_(value)
        layer.bias.zero_()
    return layer

def solve(model):
    return {name:value.clone() for name,value in model.state_dict().items()}

print(solve(fixed_linear(2.)))

lessons.title: Load values into compatible layers
explanation: Loading a state dict copies named values into an existing model with compatible shapes.
`layer.load_state_dict(state)` checks names and shapes. Use `.eval()` and no_grad to compare inference outputs.

learn.misconception: Ignoring missing or mismatched weights can leave parts of a model uninitialized.
learn.overview: Loading a state dict copies named values into an existing model with compatible shapes.
goals: Load a supplied state dictionary into an existing layer and check its output.
List what must match before loading. Why are matching filenames insufficient?

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: Saved values do not define the layer architecture by themselves. To restore a model, first construct compatible modules, then copy the named stored values into them.
The architecture configuration, tokenizer convention, mode, and weights together determine reproducible inference behavior.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Load a supplied state dictionary into an existing layer and check its output.
load_state_dict checks expected names and tensor shapes. A weight with the right number of elements but the wrong orientation is not automatically a compatible layer.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: A Linear layer expecting weight [2,3] needs that named shape in the checkpoint. After loading, a fixed input should reproduce the saved model’s output under matching evaluation settings.
`layer.load_state_dict(state)` checks names and shapes. Use `.eval()` and no_grad to compare inference outputs.

    layer.load_state_dict({"weight":torch.tensor([[float(weight)]]),"bias":torch.tensor([float(bias)])})

explanation: A checkpoint serializes model state. Load only trusted files; tensor-only loading narrows what PyTorch deserializes.

learn.overview: A checkpoint serializes model state. Load only trusted files; tensor-only loading narrows what PyTorch deserializes.
goals: Save a tensor state to an in-memory binary file and load it back on CPU.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: An in-memory dictionary disappears when the process ends. Serialization writes its tensor state so another process can restore it later.
The same state format can be written to disk. map_location="cpu" makes the small restoration independent of the original storage device.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Save a tensor state to an in-memory binary file and load it back on CPU.
io.BytesIO acts like a file in memory. Saving advances its cursor, so seek(0) rewinds before loading. weights_only=True restricts deserialization; use trusted checkpoints.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: After torch.save writes a state dictionary into the buffer, torch.load reads from its current position. Rewinding allows the loader to read the beginning instead of the end.
`torch.save(state,buffer)` and `torch.load(buffer,weights_only=True,map_location="cpu")` support an in-memory file. seek(0) rewinds it.

lessons.title: Ignore padded loss targets
explanation: Padding after a real end token should not repeatedly teach the model that all padded positions are real output.
Use an explicit valid-position mask with `.masked_fill(~valid,-100)`. -100 is the default cross-entropy ignore index.

learn.misconception: Masking every end-token ID would also hide the real termination target.
learn.overview: Padding after a real end token should not repeatedly teach the model that all padded positions are real output.
goals: Replace invalid target positions with the ignore index while preserving real targets.
Explain why replacing every occurrence of a shared end/pad ID could accidentally remove a real training target.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: Padding is added for rectangular storage, not because the training text really repeats a pad token. Supervising every padded position would change the learning objective.
The first meaningful end token can remain supervised while later padding is ignored. The validity policy must be defined during batch preparation.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Replace invalid target positions with the ignore index while preserving real targets.
An explicit boolean validity mask distinguishes content from artificial fill. masked_fill(~valid,-100) changes labels only where supervision should be omitted.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: Targets [4,9,0,0] with validity [True,True,False,False] become [4,9,-100,-100]. Token identity alone cannot decide validity when a special ID also has a legitimate use.
Use an explicit valid-position mask with `.masked_fill(~valid,-100)`. -100 is the default cross-entropy ignore index.

def solve(targets, valid):
    return targets.masked_fill(~valid, -100)

explanation: Ignoring a target removes that position from the mean loss, rather than treating the ignore value as a class.
`F.cross_entropy(...,ignore_index=-100)` skips those labels. At least one supervised position is required here.

learn.misconception: An all-ignored batch has no supervised examples; guard it instead of interpreting NaN as successful learning.
learn.overview: Ignoring a target removes that position from the mean loss, rather than treating the ignore value as a class.
goals: Compute cross-entropy using only nonignored target positions.
Add ignored positions around an unchanged valid prediction. Should its reported mean loss change?

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: Marking targets with -100 is only useful if the loss interprets that sentinel as excluded supervision. It is not a real vocabulary class.
This connects batch validity masks to the actual objective, so variable padding amounts do not teach artificial continuations or distort the mean.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Compute cross-entropy using only nonignored target positions.
With ignore_index=-100, ignored positions contribute neither a target penalty nor an item to the ordinary mean’s denominator. At least one valid target is needed in this exercise.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: If one real target has loss 2 and three other positions are ignored, mean loss remains 2, not 0.5. Padding should not dilute the reported average.
`F.cross_entropy(...,ignore_index=-100)` skips those labels. At least one supervised position is required here.

def solve(logits, targets):
    return F.cross_entropy(logits,targets,ignore_index=-100)

goals: Rescale a gradient vector only when its norm exceeds a maximum.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: An unusually large gradient can cause an oversized update. Gradient clipping limits the combined magnitude before the optimizer consumes those derivatives.
In a training loop, clip after backward has produced gradients and before optimizer.step applies them. Real model clipping combines all selected parameter gradients.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Rescale a gradient vector only when its norm exceeds a maximum.
Multiplying every component by the same factor preserves direction. Clipping each component independently would produce a different direction and a different norm guarantee.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: Gradient [3.,4.] has norm 5. With maximum norm 2.5, multiply by 0.5 to get [1.5,2.]. A gradient already below the bound should remain unchanged.
For a vector g, use `g * min(1,max_norm/(norm+epsilon))`. Clip after backward and before step.
sections.code:
def solve(g, max_norm):
    norm = torch.linalg.vector_norm(g)
    scale = torch.clamp(max_norm/(norm+1e-12),max=1.)
    return g * scale

lessons.title: Add a scaled adapter to a frozen projection
explanation: The adapter changes a base linear transformation through an additive low-rank contribution.
`base + scale*(x @ a @ b)` preserves the frozen path. Store the scale convention explicitly in configuration.

learn.misconception: Different libraries may define scale as alpha or alpha/rank; preserve the selected convention.
learn.overview: The adapter changes a base linear transformation through an additive low-rank contribution.
goals: Add a scaled low-rank update to the unchanged base projection.
Set scale to zero, then set one adapter factor to zero. What should happen in each case?

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: A low-rank update needs to be integrated with a pretrained transformation. An additive adapter lets the base remain available while learning a controlled adjustment.
Freezing base weights and optimizing only adapter factors changes which state is trainable. Libraries may express scale directly or derive it from alpha/rank.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Add a scaled low-rank update to the unchanged base projection.
The base path computes x @ weight; the adapter computes x @ A @ B. Scaling controls the adapter’s contribution and must match the convention used in training and saved configuration.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: For scalar x=2, base weight 3, A=1, B=2, and scale 0.5, the base gives 6 and the adapter contributes 2, totaling 8. A zero adapter leaves the base output intact.
`base + scale*(x @ a @ b)` preserves the frozen path. Store the scale convention explicitly in configuration.

def solve(x, weight, a, b, scale):
    return x @ weight + scale*(x @ a @ b)

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: A language model is a numerical system for scoring possible continuations of text. In this course we build a GPT-style model that repeatedly predicts one next token.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: Training has access to the full text, while generation has only the prefix generated so far. A next-token model must obey the same information boundary in both settings.
Parallel computation is compatible with causality because the mask controls which values influence each position, independently of when arithmetic is scheduled.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Explain why causal attention hides later positions even in a parallel training pass.
Without masking, a position could read the token it is supposed to predict. That would make training artificially easy and teach a behavior unavailable at generation time.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: In [A,B,C], the position holding A predicts B and may read A. The position holding B predicts C and may read A and B. Neither may read its future answer through attention.
Bidirectional encoders can use surrounding context for representation tasks.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: CPU and accelerators are places where numerical computations execute. Moving a model to a faster device is a placement decision, not a different language-model architecture.
The tiny labs run on CPU so accelerator hardware is optional. Larger training runs may benefit from device-specific setup and memory planning.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Explain how to keep model state and inputs on compatible available devices.

Module movement handles registered parameters and buffers, but not unrelated input variables. Operations combining those values need compatible placement, and device availability must be checked first.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: If the model is on an accelerator and token IDs are on CPU, moving only a random seed or changing batch size does not repair the mismatch. Move the inputs to the model’s device.

lessons.title: What distributed data parallelism does
explanation: Data-parallel training gives each process a model replica and a different shard of examples, then synchronizes gradients.
Processes need coordinated initialization, device assignment, and cleanup.

learn.overview: Data-parallel training gives each process a model replica and a different shard of examples, then synchronizes gradients.
goals: Identify the data sharding and gradient synchronization needed for coordinated replica updates.
Trace one synchronized update with two workers: data assignment, local computation, communication, and stepping.

sections.heading: Background: where this fits
points: When one device is insufficient for training throughput, data parallelism lets several processes compute on different examples using replicas of the same model.
A real setup also coordinates process initialization, device assignment, epoch sampling, and cleanup. This checkpoint teaches the responsibility of each piece without requiring multiple GPUs.

sections.heading: What we are trying to do — and why
points: Identify the data sharding and gradient synchronization needed for coordinated replica updates.

Each worker computes local gradients; synchronization combines their contributions before equivalent optimizer updates. A distributed sampler assigns example shards rather than giving every worker the entire dataset.

sections.heading: Walk through the idea
points: Two workers processing different halves of a batch must coordinate gradients so their replicas remain aligned. Two independent unsynchronized runs produce separate models, even with the same starting seed.
Processes need coordinated initialization, device assignment, and cleanup.

learn.takeaway: Identify the data sharding and gradient synchronization needed for coordinated replica updates.
learn.tryIt: Trace one synchronized update with two workers: data assignment, local computation, communication, and stepping.
learn.misconception: Identical initial seeds do not synchronize independent training runs. Data-parallel replicas need coordinated gradient updates.
